title: Only say the word (Matthew 8:5–13)
hook: a Roman officer asks healing for his servant and says he isn't worthy to have Jesus under his roof

segments.voice: Yesterday, the woman at the well: a long, honest conversation at noon. Your line was he waited at the well. What true thing did you say? Day thirty-nine.

If you've ever been to a Catholic Mass, you've heard today's story, even if you didn't know it. Just before Communion, the whole church says a line together, a line about a roof. It comes from a Roman soldier. Picture him: a centurion, an officer over about a hundred men, part of the army that occupies the country. He's used to giving orders. People step aside when he walks by. And one day in Capernaum he comes up to a Jewish teacher from the hill country, and he asks for help. Not for himself. For his servant, who is lying at home, paralyzed and suffering terribly. Today: the soldier's sentence that ended up in the Mass.
screen: `A LINE SAID BEFORE COMMUNION.` → `A ROMAN OFFICER.` → `HE ASKS FOR HIS SERVANT.`

segments.voice: Jesus answers at once: I will come and heal him. And the officer stops him. In the Douay-Rheims: "Lord, I am not worthy that thou shouldst enter under my roof: but only say the word, and my servant shall be healed." Then he explains, like a soldier. He says: I'm a man under authority myself, with soldiers under me. I say to one, go, and he goes. To another, come, and he comes. He understands how a word works when it comes from someone with authority. You don't have to walk across town. Just say it. Matthew says Jesus marveled. It's one of only two times in the Gospels that Jesus is said to be amazed, and the other time it's at people's lack of faith. He turns to the crowd following him: "Amen I say to you, I have not found so great faith in Israel." A foreigner, an officer of the occupying army, and he's the one held up as the example. Then Jesus tells him: go, and as you have believed, so be it done to you. And the servant is healed in that same hour. Now the Mass. For more than a thousand years, in Latin, Catholics have borrowed this man's words just before Communion, changing only one thing: instead of my servant, my soul. Lord, I am not worthy that you should enter under my roof, but only say the word, and my soul shall be healed. The roof is now the person. A soldier's humble sentence has become the whole Church's.
screen: `I AM NOT WORTHY. ONLY SAY THE WORD.` · `A MAN UNDER AUTHORITY.` · `JESUS MARVELED.` · `MY SERVANT BECOMES MY SOUL.` · then, large: `ONLY SAY THE WORD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Settle and breathe. Let the soldier's sentence move through you slowly: I am not worthy. But only say the word. Notice both halves. The first is honest. The second trusts. Hold them together for a few breaths. If you go to Mass, listen for this line next time, and notice the whole room saying it at once. If you pray, you can say it now, quietly, for yourself or for someone you're worried about. If not, just let it sit. The bell holds the time.
Only say the word. A Roman officer's trust, now said by Catholics at every Mass before Communion. Today's word.
Your line: only say the word. Today, carry the soldier's two halves: honest about yourself, and trusting anyway. Day thirty-nine.

screen: `DAY 39 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE HEM OF HIS CLOAK.`

howItsDone: At every Mass, just before Communion, the congregation says together a response adapted from the centurion's words, asking to be healed in soul.

original.note: Latin: Lord, I am not worthy. The opening of the words said before Communion in the Latin Mass.

trapdoor: what you thought: just something said at Mass before Communion.
what it means: a Roman officer's words, humble and trusting, held up by Jesus as great faith.
what a scholar hears: the Latin rite has said the centurion's words for centuries, changing puer meus, my servant, into anima mea, my soul.
